Triggers.value: Weapons or objects used as weapons

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
I distract myself with something else
Being emotionally close or intimate with others

Threat.value: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
I only feel safe in a very limited number of places

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

vignette: Elias was twenty-two when his village was overrun. He remembers the heavy hand on his shoulder yanking him toward the road, the glint of rifles pointed at his family, and the deafening roar of soldiers screaming orders. Those moments carved specific triggers into his nervous system: the sudden brush of a stranger's arm now feels like a seizure, the metallic click of a bag zipper echoes gun mechanisms, and a raised voice in public sends his spine rigid. Each time those triggers breached his awareness, Elias instinctively retreated into maladaptive habits. When a congregant reached out to hug him unexpectedly at the synagogue gates, the jolt of contact would immediately spark punishment thinking, driving him to mentally rehearse apologies for survival choices he never made. Simultaneously, the sudden shouting of a street vendor pushed him to rely on distraction, burying himself in administrative paperwork to numb the physical alarm before it could take hold. The relentless assault of those sensory triggers also taught him that his own physiology was fundamentally untrustworthy. Every unexpected touch or distant shout reinforced the conviction that his body kept reacting as if he were still trapped in the raid, and he began to believe he simply could not rely on himself to navigate the world without triggering. He clung to the quiet certainty that if only someone stronger had been with him back then, the violence would have been stopped, a thought that now colored every moment of perceived vulnerability. Because he viewed his mind and body as hostile, Elias's daily existence narrowed into a rigid architecture of safety. He could only feel secure in a handful of familiar rooms, and when he entered a new space like the community center or the synagogue sanctuary, he mapped his seating choices around escape routes. This constant environmental scanning fractured his ability to concentrate, turning sermons and council meetings into frustrating exercises in divided attention. The belief that he could not rely on himself actively sharpened his sensitivity to danger cues. As his internal warnings grew louder, even neutral events began to register as threats; a raised hand during a casual greeting or a door slamming down the hall would immediately register as weapons or shouting, his mind fast-forwarding to the raid before his conscious thoughts could intervene. The relentless hyper-vigilance and fractured concentration inevitably pushed him toward emotional withdrawal. When the compulsion to only feel safe in limited places made the outside world feel like a minefield, he found himself avoiding intimacy with his partner, keeping her at an emotional distance to prevent overwhelming panic. He would distract himself with prolonged Torah study to bypass the exhaustion of constant scanning, a pattern that slowly eroded their marital closeness. As the difficulty concentrating and the need to control his environment worsened, Elias's negative self-assessments hardened into dogma. The frequent lapses in focus during services convinced him that his mind was breaking down under his own flawed biology, deepening the body as enemy narrative. His need to always choose a protected seat further convinced him that he was fundamentally incapable of coping independently, leaving the others would cope belief as his only refuge. The narrowed perception effectively tuned his nervous system to anticipate violence. Because his threat monitoring was permanently elevated, the threshold for perceiving danger dropped; a sudden tap on his back from a fellow rabbi or the distant sound of construction equipment would instantly be categorized as unexpected touch or weapons, his brain skipping directly to the violent soundtrack. His reliance on punishment thinking and avoidance only cemented his most destructive self-beliefs. By constantly telling himself he deserved to suffer and deliberately pushing his partner away, he removed any opportunity to disprove his own doubts, ensuring that the can't rely on self and others would cope appraisals grew heavier with each passing month. The very habits he deployed to survive began to amplify his vulnerability to the original triggers. When he forced himself to distract through dense study or pushed people away, he never processed the underlying alarm, leaving his nervous system hypersensitive; a casual touch or a loud noise would strike with renewed intensity, his avoidance and self-punishment ensuring the trauma's echoes remained sharp. Now sixty-three, Elias sits in his modest rabbinic office, the leather chair positioned firmly against the wall. He finally came to his therapist's office after his partner packed a bag, unable to bear the wall he kept building, and after a Shabbat service where his mind went blank during the kiddush. He is terrified that his body will never stop fighting a war that ended decades ago, but he is quietly hoping someone can help him untangle the survival reflexes from his present life, so he can finally rest.
